procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Civil Appeal No. 13!5 68 was decided on 9.1.69 for the petitioner (in E. P. No. 1 of 1969). Civil 'Appeal No. 683 of 1968 was decided on August 12, 1968.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached to determine whether the nomination paper of Phul Singh, the petitioner, was wrongly rejected and whether the nomination papers of other individuals were wrongly rejected or accepted.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioners are entitled to dispute the election of the respondent on grounds other than those mentioned in section 18 of the Act.

facts: The petitioners sought to challenge the respondent's election on grounds that were not listed in section 18 of the Act.
law: The petitioners' argument was based on the plea that Part III of the Act, which includes section 18, was unconstitutional (ultra vires Article 71(1) of the Constitution) because it limited the grounds for challenging an election.
application: The Court rejected the petitioners' argument. It referred to its finding on a related issue (Issue No. 5), where it had already determined that Part III of the Act was constitutionally valid.
The Court held that Parliament did not act contrary to the Constitution when it limited the grounds for an election challenge by enumerating them in section 18 of the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because section 18 of the Act is constitutionally valid, the petitioners are not entitled to dispute the election on any grounds other than those specifically mentioned in that section. The issue was therefore answered in the negative and against the petitioners.

issue.issue_text: Whether Part III of the Act, which includes section 18, is ultra vires Art. 71 (1) of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioners argued that Part III of the Act, which includes section 18, is unconstitutional.
Their plea was that the Act improperly curtails the Supreme Court's jurisdiction by limiting the grounds on which a presidential election can be challenged.
They contended this limitation violates the broad power granted to the Court under Article 71(1) of the Constitution to inquire into and decide 'all doubts and disputes' related to the election.
law: Article 71(1) of the Constitution grants the Supreme Court exclusive jurisdiction to inquire into and decide all doubts and disputes arising from the election of a President or Vice-President.
Article 71(3) of the Constitution empowers Parliament to make laws to regulate any matter relating to or connected with the election of a President or Vice-President.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that while Article 71(1) establishes its jurisdiction, Article 71(3) allows Parliament to regulate the *manner* in which that jurisdiction is exercised.
The Court held that Parliament's power to regulate includes the authority to lay down the specific grounds on which an election can be challenged in an election petition.

Therefore, by enumerating the grounds for challenge in section 18 (part of Part III of the Act), Parliament was not unconstitutionally curtailing the Court's jurisdiction but was validly regulating the process under its powers from Article 71(3).
The Court also rejected a comparison to Article 329(b), stating that the structure of Article 71 does not limit Parliament's power to regulate the grounds for an election petition.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' contention and held that Part III of the Act is not ultra vires Article 71(1) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the election of the respondent is void on the ground of commission of a number of offences of undue influence under section 18(1)(a) and (b)(1) of the Act.

facts: The petitioners challenged the validity of the respondent's election.
The basis for the challenge was the allegation that the respondent and his supporters, with his connivance, had committed the offense of undue influence.
law: The legal ground for the challenge was section 18(1)(a) and (b)(1) of the Act, which deals with voiding an election due to the commission of undue influence.
application: To resolve the issue, the Supreme Court broke down the allegation of undue influence into three specific questions:
1. Whether the returned candidate (the respondent) personally committed the offense of undue influence.
2. Whether the offense was committed by the respondent's workers, and if so, whether it was done with his connivance.
3. Whether the offense was committed by other persons without the respondent's connivance, and if so, whether that materially affected the result of the election.
reasoning.conclusion: The provided text outlines the analytical framework the Court used to assess the claim of undue influence. While the text does not contain the specific reasoning or evidence evaluated, it shows that the Court structured its inquiry around these three key questions before ultimately rejecting the petitioners' claim.

appellant_arguments: The petitioner alleged that the respondent, Shri Giri, or other persons (like the Prime Minister) with his connivance, committed offences of undue influence.

cases.principle: The right to stand for election and the right to move for setting aside an election are not common law rights; they are statutory rights and can only be enforced in accordance with the conditions laid down in the statute.

To reject the argument that the Act and its Rules are void because they derogate from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 71(1) by placing restrictions on how an election can be challenged.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The government's rule-making power, when delegated by an Act of Parliament, is not unguided or arbitrary because it is inherently limited by the purposes of the parent Act.
obiter: The court is bound by its own previous rulings.
The law requires proof, and the extent or content of that proof is not always provided by the legislature.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitions are dismissed because the petitioners failed to prove the allegations of corrupt practice to the required standard of beyond a reasonable doubt. The court found that the statutory framework governing the election, specifically Part III of the Act, is constitutionally valid as the powers it grants are not unguided but are limited by the purposes of the Act. Furthermore, the court determined that some of the petitioners' allegations, even if accepted as true, would not legally constitute a corrupt practice, as the Act itself proceeds on the assumption that a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is permissible.
legal_tests_applied: The court must be able to come to the conclusion beyond any reasonable doubt as to the commission of the corrupt practice.
A statutory power is not unguided or arbitrary if it is limited by the purposes of the Act that grants it.
In statutory interpretation, a subsequent provision is not intended to cut down the generality of the meaning of the preceding provision.

A statute's provisions must be interpreted in light of its other subsections; for instance, a subsection that proceeds on the assumption that a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is permissible informs the definition of a corrupt practice.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioners' specific allegations of undue influence were held to have not been proven.
The court determined that some of the petitioners' allegations, even if accepted as true, did not legally constitute an offence under the Act.

The petitioners' arguments were undermined by the court's interpretation that the Act proceeds on the assumption that a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action does not constitute a corrupt practice.
why_respondent_won: The petitioners failed to meet the high standard of proof required, which is proof beyond a reasonable doubt for the commission of a corrupt practice.

The court upheld the constitutionality of the Act's provisions, finding that the rule-making power conferred by Parliament was not unguided or arbitrary because it was limited by the purposes of the Act itself.
The court's interpretation of the statute established that the actions alleged by the petitioners, such as declarations of public policy, were not prohibited.
policy_considerations: However onerous the task of the court may be because of the partisan nature of the witnesses, it cannot reject the oral evidence adduced merely on that ground, but it has to examine the same carefully and come to a conclusion.
